levels.title_en: Feelings: the adjectives that never change

items.pronunciation_notes: The dotted ख़ is further back in the throat than a plain ख, closer to the ch in Scottish loch. One syllable, no vowel at the end.

learn.explanation_en: ख़ुश means happy, and it is an unmarked adjective, so it never changes: मैं ख़ुश हूँ, वह ख़ुश है, वे ख़ुश हैं. Module 6 taught you that adjectives ending in -ा take three forms and everything else takes one. ख़ुश ends in a consonant, so it belongs to the second group and you can stop thinking about agreement entirely. That is true of most emotion adjectives in Hindi, which makes this a comfortable block to start Module 8 with.

examples.note: The adjective is identical whoever is speaking.
बहुत intensifies it, and still nothing changes.
With होना's perfective it means became rather than were.

common_error.why_en: ख़ुशी is the noun happiness. The adjective is ख़ुश, and adding -ी to it does not make it feminine — it makes it a different word.

practice.question: ख़ुश
practice.explanation_en: ख़ुश is happy. It is an adjective and never changes its form.

game.explanation_en: ख़ुश होना — to be or become happy. ख़ुश करना exists but means to make someone else happy.

items.pronunciation_notes: Aspirated kh in the middle and a long ii at the end: du-khii.

learn.title_en: दुखी ends in -ी and is still unmarked
learn.explanation_en: This is the trap worth catching early. दुखी ends in -ी, which after Module 6 makes it look like a feminine form waiting for a masculine partner. It is not. दुखी is invariable, so a man is दुखी and so is a woman: वह दुखी है either way. A whole family of adjectives borrowed from Sanskrit behaves this way — दुखी, सुखी, ज़रूरी, ख़ाली — and none of them has a -ा form at all. Only adjectives that actually end in -ा take the three-way agreement.

examples.note: Said of a man, and the form is unchanged.
A feminine subject, and still दुखी.
Plural and past, and the adjective does not follow.

common_error.why_en: There is no दुखा. Working backwards from the -ी to invent a masculine form is the mistake this word invites.

practice.question: दुखी
practice.explanation_en: दुखी is sad. It looks feminine and is in fact invariable.

game.explanation_en: दुखी होना — to be or become sad.

items.pronunciation_notes: Three syllables with the stress on the last, which carries a long aa: pa-re-shaan.

learn.explanation_en: परेशान covers a wide range that English splits up: worried, bothered, troubled, hassled, at the end of your patience. It is a Persian borrowing, it ends in a consonant, and it never changes. Two verbs go with it and they mean opposite things. परेशान होना is to be worried; परेशान करना is to bother someone else, and it is what a parent says to a child who will not sit still. Getting those two the wrong way round reverses who is troubling whom.

examples.note: The state, with होना.
With करना the meaning flips — he is doing it to me.
The negative imperative from Module 7, and a very common sentence.

common_error.why_en: करना makes you the source of the trouble rather than the one feeling it. For your own state the verb is होना.

practice.question: परेशान
practice.explanation_en: परेशान is worried or bothered, and it covers more ground than any single English word.

game.question_en: Which verb goes with परेशान when you mean your own state?
game.explanation_en: परेशान होना is to be worried. परेशान करना would mean you are bothering someone else.

summary.recap_en: Most emotion adjectives in Hindi are unmarked and never change, including दुखी, which ends in -ी and still does not. Only adjectives ending in -ा take the three-way agreement from Module 6. Watch the verb that goes with each one — होना for your own state, करना for doing it to someone else.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the nouns behind these states, and two of them that arrive rather than being felt.

items.pronunciation_notes: The same throaty ख़ as ख़ुश, with a long ii added: khu-shii.

learn.explanation_en: ख़ुशी is happiness, feminine, and predictably so because it ends in -ी. Hindi builds a lot of abstract nouns this way, adding -ी to an adjective, so ख़ुश gives ख़ुशी and the pattern will recur. Its oblique plural is ख़ुशियाँ, following Class 4 exactly as लड़की did. The sentence you will meet it in most is मुझे ख़ुशी हुई — literally happiness happened to me, which is how Hindi says I was glad.

examples.note: The verb agrees with ख़ुशी, which is feminine — hence हुई.

examples.english: it is a matter of great joy
examples.note: बड़ी and की both agree with the feminine nouns in front of them.
The bare noun, with होना in the present.

common_error.why_en: The verb agrees with ख़ुशी, not with मुझे. ख़ुशी is feminine, so the perfective is हुई.

practice.question: ख़ुशी
practice.explanation_en: ख़ुशी is happiness — the noun formed from the adjective ख़ुश.

game.explanation_en: ख़ुशी होना — happiness happens to you, which is how Hindi expresses being glad.

items.pronunciation_notes: The dotted ग़ is made further back than a plain ग, and the स is doubled and held: gus-saa.

learn.title_en: Anger comes to you rather than being felt
learn.explanation_en: The natural way to say I got angry in Hindi is मुझे ग़ुस्सा आया — anger came to me. The emotion is the subject and the person experiencing it is marked with को, which is why मुझे appears rather than मैं. That shape covers a whole family of feelings and you have already seen it with ख़ुशी. ग़ुस्सा करना also exists but means something narrower: to direct anger at someone. So आना for the feeling arriving, करना for the behaviour.

examples.note: आया agrees with ग़ुस्सा, which is masculine.
The habitual — this happens to him regularly.
With करना and a negative imperative from Module 7.

common_error.why_en: The one who feels it takes को, so मैं becomes मुझे. The verb agrees with ग़ुस्सा instead.

practice.question: ग़ुस्सा
practice.explanation_en: ग़ुस्सा is anger, and it is masculine despite being an abstract noun.

game.question_en: Which verb goes with ग़ुस्सा when the feeling arrives?
game.explanation_en: ग़ुस्सा आना — anger comes. ग़ुस्सा करना is to direct it at someone.

items.pronunciation_notes: Retroflex ड with the tongue curled back, then a light r: ḍar, one syllable.

learn.title_en: डर — masculine, and it attaches rather than arrives
learn.explanation_en: डर is fear. It ends in a consonant so nothing tells you its gender and you have to learn it as masculine — this is the first flagged word of Module 8 and there will be more. Its verb is लगना, which is a third pattern alongside होना and आना: मुझे डर लगता है, fear attaches to me. There is no rule deciding which emotion takes which verb, which is exactly why the game card in this module asks about collocation rather than gender. The pairings have to be learnt with the word.

examples.note: लगता agrees with डर, which is masculine.
The perfective — लगना is intransitive, so no ने is involved.
Here डर is the verb डरना in its तू imperative, not the noun.

common_error.why_en: होना is not the verb for this noun. Each emotion word carries its own verb, and डर takes लगना.

practice.question: डर
practice.explanation_en: डर is fear, and it is masculine — worth memorising, since the ending gives you nothing.

game.explanation_en: डर लगना — fear attaches to you. Not होना, and not आना.

summary.recap_en: Emotion nouns in Hindi mostly happen to you rather than being felt by you: the feeling is the subject and the person takes को. Which verb goes with which noun is not predictable — ख़ुशी होना, ग़ुस्सा आना, डर लगना — so the pairing is part of learning the word.
summary.next_up_en: Next: love, laughter and rest, and the three verbs that go with them.

items.pronunciation_notes: One syllable, with the p and y run together and a long aa: pyaar.

learn.title_en: प्यार — the one that takes करना
learn.explanation_en: प्यार is love or affection, masculine and flagged because the consonant ending tells you nothing. Unlike the last three, this one takes करना, and it is transitive: you love someone, and the person loved is marked with से. वह मुझसे प्यार करता है — he loves me, literally does love from me. That से catches learners out, because English uses no preposition there at all. प्यार is uncountable, so it has no plural.

examples.note: मुझसे is मैं fused with से, from Module 6.

examples.hindi: माँ बच्चों से प्यार करती है
examples.read_as: maaṁ bachchoṁ se pyaar kartii hai
examples.note: बच्चों is the oblique plural before से.
Here से makes प्यार into a manner — with love.

common_error.why_en: प्यार करना takes से for the person loved, not को. मुझे would be the को form, which belongs with other verbs.

practice.question: प्यार
practice.explanation_en: प्यार is love, masculine, and it has no plural.

game.explanation_en: प्यार करना — and the person loved takes से rather than को.

tts_strings: माँ बच्चों से प्यार करती है

items.pronunciation_notes: The nasal sits on the first syllable as a hum, not a full n: haṁ-sii.

learn.title_en: हँसी — and the verb it comes from
learn.explanation_en: हँसी is laughter, feminine and predictable from its -ी ending. It comes from हँसना, to laugh, which is a verb you can use directly: वह हँसता है, he laughs. The noun takes आना like ग़ुस्सा does, and मुझे हँसी आई means something English needs a whole phrase for — I couldn't help laughing, it struck me as funny. Having both the verb and the noun available is common in this module and worth noticing: one describes the act, the other describes the feeling arriving.

examples.note: आई agrees with हँसी, which is feminine.
The verb हँसना, used directly with a plain subject.
The continuous past from Module 7, on the same verb.

common_error.why_en: हँसी is feminine, so the perfective is आई. The verb agrees with the feeling, never with the person.

practice.question: हँसी
practice.explanation_en: हँसी is laughter, from the verb हँसना.

game.explanation_en: हँसी आना — laughter comes to you, the same shape as ग़ुस्सा आना.

items.pronunciation_notes: Two long aa vowels bracketing a light r: aa-raam.

learn.explanation_en: आराम is rest, and it stretches to cover comfort and relief as well. आराम करना is to rest, and it is the standard thing to tell someone who is unwell. The word also turns up as an adverb in आराम से, which means slowly, calmly, take your time — one of the most useful two-word phrases in the language, and the polite way to tell someone not to rush. Masculine, flagged, and uncountable.

examples.note: The तुम imperative from Module 7.
The continuous present, with करना as the verb.
आराम से means calmly or unhurriedly, and the imperative is polite.

common_error.why_en: Rest is something you do rather than something that happens to you, so this noun takes करना.

practice.question: आराम
practice.explanation_en: आराम is rest or comfort, and आराम से means calmly.

game.explanation_en: आराम करना — rest is done rather than received.

summary.recap_en: Three nouns and three different verbs: प्यार करना, हँसी आना, आराम करना. Two of them also give you set phrases worth knowing whole — प्यार से for kindly and आराम से for calmly, both built with से.
summary.next_up_en: Next: the rest of the emotion block, including one adjective that does change and one noun whose gender you would guess wrong.

items.pronunciation_notes: The first syllable is short and the second long: u-daas.

learn.explanation_en: Both mean sad and they are not interchangeable. दुखी is closer to unhappy or grieved and points at a cause — someone is दुखी about something. उदास is closer to low or downcast, a mood rather than a response, and it is the word songs and poetry reach for. If you are describing how someone looks rather than what has happened to them, उदास is usually the better choice. Like दुखी, it is unmarked and never changes.

examples.note: A mood, with no cause implied.
क्यों from Module 5, and तुम takes हो.
Plural and past, and the adjective is unchanged.

common_error.why_en: उदासी is the noun, meaning sadness. The adjective is उदास, exactly as ख़ुश stands to ख़ुशी.

practice.question: उदास
practice.explanation_en: उदास is downcast or low — a mood rather than a reaction to something.

game.explanation_en: उदास होना. Adjectives of state generally take होना; it is the nouns that vary.

items.pronunciation_notes: Aspirated th at the front, which is not the th of English think: tha-kaa.

learn.title_en: The one in this block that does change
learn.explanation_en: थका is tired, and unlike every other word in these four levels it ends in -ा and therefore agrees: थका, थकी, थके. That is because it is not really an adjective at all — it is the perfective participle of थकना, to get tired, being used as one. Module 7 showed the same thing with बैठा है meaning he is sitting: the action is finished and the resulting state is what you are describing. So वह थका है is he is tired, and the agreement comes from the participle it started life as.

examples.note: Said by a man. A woman says थकी.
The feminine form, agreeing like any marked adjective.
Plural and past, and both words agree.

common_error.why_en: If the subject is a woman the adjective is थकी. This is the only word in the emotion block that requires that choice.

practice.question: थका
practice.explanation_en: थका is tired, and it agrees with the subject because it began as a participle.

game.question_en: Which verb does थका come from?
game.explanation_en: थकना, to get tired. थका is its perfective participle used as an adjective.

items.pronunciation_notes: The nasal is written with a dot and sounds as an n before the त: chin-taa.

learn.title_en: चिंता ends in -ा and is feminine
learn.explanation_en: This is the gender trap of the block. चिंता ends in -ा, which after Module 4 and Module 6 should say masculine to you, and it is feminine. A group of nouns borrowed from Sanskrit behaves this way — चिंता, भाषा, सभा — and none of them is predictable from its ending, so they have to be memorised as pairs. The consequence shows up immediately in agreement: बड़ी चिंता, not बड़ा, and its plural is चिंताएँ rather than चिंते. The phrase to over-learn is चिंता मत करो, do not worry.

examples.note: Probably the most-used sentence this word appears in.
The feeling with होना, and the person marked with को.

examples.english: it is a matter of real concern
examples.note: बड़ी and की both agree with feminine nouns — the proof that चिंता is feminine.

common_error.why_en: The -ा ending is misleading. चिंता is feminine, so any marked adjective in front of it takes -ी.

practice.question: चिंता
practice.explanation_en: चिंता is worry, and it is feminine despite the -ा ending.

game.explanation_en: चिंता करना — to worry. चिंता होना also occurs and describes the state rather than the act.

summary.recap_en: The emotion block ends with its two exceptions. थका is the only adjective here that agrees, because it is a perfective participle doing an adjective's job. चिंता is feminine despite ending in -ा, which no rule predicts and which shows up the moment an adjective stands in front of it.
summary.next_up_en: Next: weather, starting with the noun whose verb the whole module was designed to teach.

items.pronunciation_notes: Long aa in the first syllable and a soft sh at the end: baa-rish.

learn.title_en: Rain happens — it does not come
learn.explanation_en: Hindi has no verb meaning to rain. It says बारिश होना, rain happens, and the noun is the subject of the sentence. That makes बारिश हो रही है the ordinary way to say it is raining. The verb to avoid is आना: बारिश आना sounds like the rain is a visitor and is not what people say. बारिश is feminine and flagged, because the consonant ending gives you nothing, and the agreement follows from that — बारिश हुई, never हुआ.

examples.note: The continuous present, with बारिश as the subject.
The bare perfective, and हुई agrees with the feminine noun.

examples.english: do not go out in the rain
examples.note: बारिश is oblique before में, though nothing visible changes.

common_error.why_en: Rain happens rather than arrives. आना is used for people and for feelings, not for weather.

practice.question: बारिश
practice.explanation_en: बारिश is rain, and it is feminine — worth memorising, since the ending is no guide.

game.explanation_en: बारिश होना. Hindi has no verb for to rain, so the noun does the work with होना behind it.

items.pronunciation_notes: Breathy dh at the front and a long uu: dhuup, one syllable.

collocation.english: for the sun to come out

learn.title_en: धूप is the sunlight, not the sun
learn.explanation_en: धूप is sunshine — the light and warmth falling on you — and it is a different word from सूरज, the sun itself. That distinction matters, because you sit in धूप and you look at सूरज. Its verb is निकलना, to emerge: धूप निकली, the sun came out. धूप होना also works and simply states that it is sunny. Feminine and flagged, like most weather words in Hindi, which is worth noting as a pattern even though it is not a rule.

examples.note: The simplest statement, with होना.
निकली agrees with the feminine धूप.

examples.english: he is sitting in the sun
examples.note: बैठा है is the perfective describing a state, from Module 7.

common_error.why_en: धूप is feminine, so the perfective is निकली. The consonant ending makes this easy to get wrong.

practice.question: धूप
practice.explanation_en: धूप is sunshine — the light itself, as distinct from सूरज, the sun.

game.question_en: Which verb goes with धूप when the sun comes out?

items.pronunciation_notes: The two words run together in speech, with the nasal-free हुई holding its long ii.

learn.explanation_en: Weather is the easiest place to practise Module 7, because every sentence about it is built from one noun plus होना, and only the tense changes. This exchange runs through three of them: होगी for a guess about later, है for now, and हुई for yesterday. Notice that the agreement never moves — बारिश is feminine, so every form of होना that touches it is feminine too. That is the whole grammar of talking about the weather in Hindi.

common_error.why_en: बारिश is feminine, so every form of होना agreeing with it is feminine, in any tense.

practice.question: बारिश हो रही है
practice.explanation_en: The continuous present — rain is happening as you speak.

game.question_en: Listen to the last line. Which word is missing?
game.explanation_en: बारिश is feminine and singular, so the perfective is हुई.

summary.recap_en: Weather in Hindi is a noun plus a verb, not a verb of its own — बारिश होना, धूप निकलना. Both words are feminine and both are flagged, since their consonant endings predict nothing. Talking about the weather is therefore mostly a matter of choosing the tense.
summary.next_up_en: Next: wind, cold, heat and cloud, and the words for the seasons they belong to.
